name: ADS1115IDGSR
title: 16-bit, 860 SPS delta-sigma ADC with internal reference, PGA and I2C (ADS1113, ADS1114, ADS1115)
summary: A family of three tiny 16-bit delta-sigma converters with an on-chip reference and oscillator, read over I2C at one of four pin-set addresses, running from 2.0 V to 5.5 V and specified from –40 °C to +125 °C. Data rate is programmable from 8 to 860 samples per second, in continuous mode at about 150 µA or single-shot mode that powers down after each result. The ADS1113 has one differential input at ±2.048 V; the ADS1114 adds a PGA (±0.256 V to ±6.144 V) and a programmable comparator on ALERT/RDY; the ADS1115 adds a MUX for two differential or four ground-referred inputs. ADS1115IDGSR is the ADS1115 in VSSOP-10 on a 2500-piece reel.
key_figures: 150 µA typ, 200 µA max continuous at 25 °C; 0.5 µA typ power-down

circuits.title: Basic hardware configuration
circuits.description: The converter on a 3.3 V rail talking I2C to an MSP430F2002. ADDR is strapped to ground, giving address 1001000. One pair of 10 kΩ resistors pulls SCL and SDA up to 3.3 V, and each chip has 100 nF across its supply. The analog inputs and ALERT come out as terminals; AIN2 and AIN3 exist on the ADS1115 only, ALERT on the ADS1114 and ADS1115.
notes: The MSP430 SCL and SDA are its P1.6 and P1.7; it also has JTAG and serial/UART connections.

circuits.title: Typical connections of the ADS1115
circuits.description: The ADS1115 on a host's I2C port. SCL and SDA each have a pull-up to VDD of 1 kΩ to 10 kΩ, and ALERT/RDY, being open drain, has a third one and goes to a host GPIO. ADDR is tied to ground. A 0.1 µF capacitor sits on VDD to supply the short current spikes drawn while converting. The four analog inputs go out to terminals; which pair or single input is measured is set in the Config register.

parts.value: microcontroller or microprocessor with I2C port

circuits.title: Using GPIO with a single ADS1115
circuits.description: A host without an I2C peripheral runs the bus from two GPIO lines in software. GPIO_1 drives SCL directly with no pull-up, which works because the converter never pulls the clock low. GPIO_0 carries SDA and has a pull-up to VDD.

parts.value: microcontroller or microprocessor with GPIO ports

circuits.title: Connecting multiple ADS1113/4/5s
circuits.description: Four converters share one I2C bus and one pair of pull-ups (1 kΩ to 10 kΩ typical) to VDD. Each takes its own address from where its ADDR pin goes: U1 to GND, U2 to VDD, U3 to SCL and U4 to SDA.

parts.value: microcontroller or microprocessor with I2C port

circuits.title: Connecting multiple device types
circuits.description: Two ADS1115s, a TMP421 temperature sensor and a DAC8574 on one bus with a shared pair of pull-ups to VDD. The ADS1115s take addresses from ADDR at GND (U1) and at VDD (U2). The TMP421 has A1 and A0 left open, which sets 0101010. The DAC8574 has A2 high and A3, A1, A0 low, which sets 1001100.

parts.value: microcontroller or microprocessor with I2C port

circuits.title: Measuring single-ended inputs
circuits.description: The ADS1115 reading four ground-referred signals. Each input goes straight to a terminal and the MUX measures it against GND, so a signal from 0 V up to the supply gives codes 0 to 32767 over SCL and SDA, and the negative half of the code range is unused. VDD has 0.1 µF to ground.

circuits.title: Low-side current measurement
circuits.description: A shunt RS under the load drops 50 mV at full-scale current. An OPA335 on a single 5 V supply amplifies it by 4, set by 3 kΩ feedback over 1 kΩ to ground, giving 0.2 V at full scale into AIN0, with AIN1 at the shunt's ground end. R3, 49.9 kΩ from the amplifier output to −5 V, pulls down so the output can swing accurately to 0 V. The ADS1114 runs at PGA gain 16 (±0.256 V full scale) from a 2.0 V to 5 V rail with 0.1 µF, and reports over I2C.

operation.text: Each device is a 16-bit delta-sigma converter: a differential switched-capacitor modulator and a digital filter, with an on-chip voltage reference and clock oscillator and an I2C interface. The ADS1114 and ADS1115 add a PGA ahead of the modulator and a digital comparator driving ALERT/RDY; the ADS1115 also has a four-input MUX. The core always converts the difference AINP – AINN, which strongly rejects common-mode signals.

MODE selects continuous or single-shot conversion. Continuously, a new conversion starts as soon as one finishes, at the programmed data rate, and the Conversion register always holds the latest result. In single-shot mode the device waits with OS high; writing 1 to OS starts one conversion (OS reads 0 meanwhile), and when the result is ready OS returns to 1 and the part shuts down. A 1 written to OS mid-conversion does nothing. Power-down single-shot is the default.

Three Config bits pick AIN0–AIN1, AIN0–AIN3, AIN1–AIN3 or AIN2–AIN3 as differential pairs, or any one input against GND, in which case the MUX switches the negative side of the converter to GND. The ADS1113 and ADS1114 have no MUX: they measure AIN0 against AIN1, and a single-ended signal is measured by grounding AIN1.

A signal measured against ground can only produce positive codes, so the negative half of the code range goes unused, costing one bit; linearity is unaffected. The signal can run from 0 V to the supply. No input may go negative: the device reads bipolar differential signals but accepts only positive voltages on each pin.

ESD diodes to VDD and GND guard every analog input on all three devices; to keep them off, each input must stay between GND – 0.3 V and VDD + 0.3 V. Where a source could go further, Schottky clamps, series resistors or both keep the current within the absolute maximum. Overdriving an unused ADS1115 input can disturb conversions on the other inputs, so unused inputs that might be overdriven are also clamped with Schottky diodes. Inputs held more than about 300 mV past either rail for long periods can be permanently damaged; momentary currents up to 100 mA are tolerated. A front-end op amp on high supplies such as ±12 V can swing to a rail at power-up before its input settles, and that spike damages the inputs gradually, so protection is needed even when the amplifier is set up never to leave the input range.

The switched-capacitor input samples AINP and AINN onto small capacitors and discharges them to about 0.7 V (the differential capacitor to 0 V) at fCLK = 250 kHz, so the source sees an average resistive load. Common-mode impedance (both inputs shorted together) is about 6 MΩ at the default gain and changes with the PGA setting; differential impedance scales with gain and is listed in the differential input impedance table. These values cannot be ignored unless the source impedance is low; a high-impedance source may need a buffer, which in turn adds noise, offset and gain error. The impedances drift slightly with temperature because the oscillator does.

The ADS1114 and ADS1115 PGA offers gains of 2/3, 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16, selected by three Config bits, for ranges of ±6.144 V down to ±0.256 V. The ADS1113 is fixed at ±2.048 V. At gain 2/3 the input can reach the supply when VDD is above 4 V; in that case, and at gain 1 with VDD below 4 V, the full-scale code cannot be reached. The input voltage limits of the electrical table apply whatever the range.
Results are 16-bit binary twos complement. Positive full scale reads 7FFFh, negative full scale 8000h, and signals beyond full scale clip at those codes.

Input content above half the data rate aliases. The sinc digital filter attenuates high-frequency noise but is not a full anti-aliasing filter; where external filtering is needed a simple RC is enough, chosen with the converter's input impedance in mind. Signals that are slow by nature, such as a thermocouple's output, still carry noise and interference that can fold back.

Power-up performs a reset that returns every Config bit to its default. The I2C general call reset (address 0000000 with the eighth bit 0, then the byte 06h) does the same as a power-on reset: the registers are reset and the device powers down. After a reset the Conversion register reads 0 until a conversion completes.

The master can save power by setting the device to 860 SPS in single-shot mode and asking for one conversion every 125 ms, an effective 8 SPS. A conversion at 860 SPS takes about 1.2 ms, so the device is powered down for the other 123.8 ms and uses roughly one hundredth the power of continuous conversion. The duty cycle is entirely up to the master. The genuinely slow data rates do not duty-cycle and give lower noise.

The digital comparator works as a traditional or a window comparator (COMP_MODE). Traditional: ALERT/RDY goes active (low unless changed) once a result goes above Hi_thresh and releases when it drops below Lo_thresh. Window: it asserts when a result is above Hi_thresh or below Lo_thresh. COMP_LAT makes the assertion stick until the Conversion register is read or an SMBus alert response clears it. COMP_POL sets the active level. COMP_QUE asserts after one, two or four successive results beyond a threshold, or turns the comparator off. Because the comparison is digital, the threshold values need adjusting whenever the PGA setting changes. Outside conversion-ready mode, Hi_thresh must be larger than Lo_thresh.

Setting the MSB of Hi_thresh to 1 and the MSB of Lo_thresh to 0 turns ALERT/RDY into a conversion-ready output. COMP_POL still sets polarity and COMP_QUE can still turn the pin off; COMP_MODE and COMP_LAT stop having any effect, and the pin still needs a pull-up. In continuous mode the pin gives a short pulse of about 8 µs after each conversion; in single-shot mode it follows the OS bit, dropping low once a result is ready when COMP_POL = 0.

With COMP_LAT = 1, ALERT/RDY behaves as an SMBus alert. Once the master sees the line latched it sends the SMBus alert address 00011001; every ADS1114/5 with its alert asserted answers with its own address. If several answer, address arbitration picks the lowest address, which clears its alert; the losers keep theirs, and the master repeats until all are cleared. In window mode the status bit returned is 1 for a result above the high threshold and 0 for one below the low threshold. A result outside the thresholds after clearing asserts the pin again; conversions in progress are not affected. ALERT/RDY is open drain like SDA and stays high when disabled so it can share a line.

The devices are I2C slaves only: they never drive SCL, which is a pure input, and never stretch the clock. Both lines are open drain and need pull-ups. Bytes are acknowledged by the receiver pulling SDA low on the ninth clock; leaving SDA high is a not-acknowledge. The bus times out if held idle for more than 25 ms. Every read or write starts with a START and ends with a STOP.

Standard (up to 100 kHz), fast (up to 400 kHz) and high-speed (up to 3.4 MHz) modes are all supported. Standard and fast need nothing special. High-speed mode is entered by sending the Hs master code 00001xxx after a START; the device does not acknowledge it, switches its Hs filters in, and returns to normal speed at the next STOP.
ADDR is sampled continuously and connects to GND, VDD, SDA or SCL for addresses 1001000 to 1001011, so up to four devices share a bus.

Four 16-bit registers (Conversion, Config, Lo_thresh, Hi_thresh) are reached through the write-only Pointer register, whose two low bits pick one. A write is: address byte with R/W low, pointer byte, then the register's high byte and low byte, each acknowledged by the device. A read uses the last pointer value: address byte with R/W high, after which the device sends the high byte then the low byte, each acknowledged by the master, who may end after either byte with a not-acknowledge, START or STOP. To read a different register the pointer is written first (address byte, pointer byte, then STOP or repeated START); repeated reads of the same register need no new pointer. Every write includes the pointer.

With ADDR at ground (address 1001000), continuous conversion is set up and read as follows. Write the Config register: 0b10010000 (address, write), 0b00000001 (Config pointer), 0b10000100 (Config MSB), 0b10000011 (Config LSB). Point to the Conversion register: 0b10010000, 0b00000000. Read: 0b10010001 (address, read), after which the device returns the Conversion register MSB and then its LSB.

The supply needs a 0.1 µF bypass capacitor to deliver the brief current spikes drawn during conversion. SDA and SCL need pull-ups, typically 1 kΩ to 10 kΩ, sized for bus speed and capacitance: larger values save power but slow the edges and so the bus; smaller values allow higher speed for more current, but too small and the drivers cannot pull the line low. Long lines and several devices add capacitance and call for slightly smaller values. One set of pull-ups serves a whole bus. Any I2C controller works, including master-only ones; clock-stretching support is not needed unless another device on the bus stretches.

Without an I2C controller, GPIO pins can bit-bang the bus: each line is set to output 0 to pull low and switched to input to let it rise, and is read while an input. Because the converter never holds SCL low, the host can drive SCL as a push-pull output with no pull-up, which also saves current; this is not allowed if any other device on the bus can hold the clock low. A strong internal pull-up can stand in for the external resistor on some microcontrollers; weak internal pull-ups are usually not enough.

In the shunt monitor the ADS1114/5 runs at gain 8 or 16 so the op amp gain can stay low. At gain 16 the amplifier output must not exceed 0.256 V; with a 50 mV shunt drop at full current and an amplifier gain of 4 the converter sees 0.2 V at full scale.
